title: Spreadsheet Column Label
statement:
Spreadsheet columns are labelled with capital letters: A through Z for the first 26 columns, then AA, AB, …, AZ, BA, …, ZZ, then AAA, and so on.

Given a column number n (the first column is 1), return its label.

examples.why: 26 columns use one letter. Column 27 is AA, so 28 is AB.
Plain base 26 would write 52 as "2" then "0", but there is no letter for zero. The last letter is Z (26), leaving 26 for the first letter: A.
26 one-letter labels plus 26 · 26 = 676 two-letter labels end at ZZ = 702.

hints: This is almost base 26, with digits A = 1 to Z = 26. What is different about it compared with normal base 26?
There is no zero digit. If you shift every digit down by one, so A = 0 and Z = 25, it becomes ordinary base 26.
Repeat: subtract 1 from n, the last letter is n % 26, then divide n by 26.

explain.intuition:
Normal number systems have a zero digit. This one does not: its digits run from A = 1 to Z = 26. That is why 26 is Z and not "A0", and why the usual divide-and-take-the-remainder trick goes wrong on multiples of 26.

The fix is to subtract 1 before each step. Then the last digit runs from 0 to 25, which maps straight to A to Z, and dividing by 26 gives exactly the number written by the remaining letters.
steps: Start with an empty list of letters.
Append the letter 'A' + n % 26, then set n = floor(n / 26).
The letters came out last-first, so reverse them and return the string.
pitfalls: Using plain base 26. Multiples of 26 produce a remainder of 0, which has no letter, as in 52 → "AZ".
Forgetting to reverse: the remainders give the rightmost letter first.

solutions.title: Borrow when the remainder is zero
solutions.idea: Take n % 26. A remainder of 0 means the letter is Z, and you borrow one from the rest of the number.

solutions.title: Shift to zero-based base 26
solutions.idea: Subtract 1 before each step so the digit range becomes 0..25, then use ordinary base conversion.

followups: Go the other way: turn a label like "FXSHRXW" back into its column number.
Why does subtracting 1 at every step, not just once at the start, give the right answer?
